stage1/problem/A1/v0:
Problem: Can MVFA's segmentation adapters be trained without any pixel masks, using only image-level normal/abnormal labels on all six BMAD source datasets, by replacing the Dice + Focal targets with pseudo-masks derived from the frozen CLIP patch features (patches of an abnormal training image that have no close neighbour among the patches of normal images of the same dataset), and how much of the zero-shot pixel-level AUROC and Dice of the mask-supervised MVFA does this recover on a held-out modality?

Rationale: MVFA's anomaly maps come only from the segmentation adapters, which are trained with Dice and Focal losses on BrainMRI, LiverCT and RESC masks (G3); the three image-only datasets (OCT17, ChestXray, HIS) never contribute localisation supervision, and the few-shot setting additionally assumes K masked abnormal images (G4). The related work shows that weaker signals can supervise localisation: CoDeGraph [30] filters consistent anomalies with batch-level patch graphs and shows that the resulting pseudo-masks can supervise prompt-driven vision-language models; DDAD [54] exploits unlabelled abnormal images alongside normal ones; MediCLIP [10] and SpatioPrompt [20] adapt CLIP from normal images with synthetic anomalies; MedSAD-CLIP [8] instead assumes real masks. None of these tests whether MVFA's multi-level residual adapters, the target method's own component, can be trained from image-level labels alone. The question is fine-grained (one loss target of one branch), feasible on BMAD with one GPU because pseudo-masks are computed once with frozen features, and measurable under the shared protocol: pixel AUROC and Dice on BrainMRI, LiverCT and RESC when held out, compared with the re-run mask-supervised MVFA, plus the effect of adding the three mask-free datasets as localisation sources. A positive answer removes MVFA's dependence on dense expert masks; a negative one quantifies how much masks are worth.
stage1/problem/B1/v0:
Problem: Can the transductive test-set min-max normalisation, fixed 0.5 fusion weight and max-over-pixels image score of MVFA's few-shot inference be replaced by a per-image score computed only from the K-shot support images and source-modality validation data, such that image-level AUROC stays within 1 point of the re-run baseline while the scores become threshold-ready (sensitivity at 95% specificity, expected calibration error) and invariant to the composition of the test set (prevalence and outlier resampling)?

Rationale: The released code normalises each branch with the minimum and maximum over the entire test set before fusing them with weight 0.5 (G8), and the image AUC on masked datasets is the maximum of the fused map, so one spurious pixel decides the label (G9); only threshold-free AUC is reported (G11). A deployed system scores one image at a time, so the published numbers are not those of a usable detector. Recent CLIP detectors in the review set treat scoring and fusion as a design problem of its own: LaRP-CLIP [17] criticises fixed fusion strategies and global-similarity image scores, HeadCLIP [4] proposes a joint anomaly score that uses pixel-level information, and CANOR [55] shows that a handful of calibration scalars and a principled aggregation rule improve CLIP scores without retraining the encoder. None addresses the transductive normalisation that MVFA's results depend on. The problem concerns one component (the inference-time scoring of the few-shot branch), needs no retraining, runs in hours on one GPU, and has measurable outcomes: AUROC change, sensitivity at fixed specificity, ECE, and the variance of an image's score when the rest of the test set is resampled.
stage1/problem/D1/v0:
Problem: Can MVFA's few-shot patch memory bank, which stores every adapted patch feature of the K normal support images at four levels, be replaced by a compact parametric model of normal patch features per level (a small set of prototypes or a Gaussian with shrinkage covariance), and how does this change few-shot pixel- and image-level AUROC, memory footprint and per-image inference time as K grows from 2 to 16?

Rationale: MVFA compares query patches with a memory bank whose size grows linearly with K and with spatial resolution, without modelling the compact distribution of normal tissue against the diverse distribution of anomalies (G7), and its retrieval cost and the privacy implication of storing raw patient-derived features are not analysed (G13). Related work points toward explicit compact normality: AVA-DINO [14] exploits the asymmetry of compact normals versus diverse anomalies, Spatial-FAD [6] stores compact normal and abnormal prototypes to cut memory while improving few-shot localisation, and the Consistency Margin Adapter [21] aligns representations with a normal reference through margin objectives. Whether a compact normal model suffices for MVFA's adapted features has not been tested. The question isolates one component (the few-shot comparison against stored normals), is feasible because it needs no retraining of the adapters, and has measurable outcomes: AUROC differences relative to the full bank, bytes stored per support image, latency, and the K at which the compact model matches the bank.
